1:
Who the Grecians were takes up most of the comment. Ellicott insists the English word is always Grecians and never Greeks, since these are Greek-speaking Jews of the dispersion, who read the Septuagint and as a rule neither read Hebrew nor spoke the current Aramaic; by this date they may have outnumbered the Hebrews, and were commonly more zealous for the holy places, with the zeal of pilgrims, than the Jews of Jerusalem who had known them from infancy. Robertson adds that they touched the Gentile world without adopting its habits. Lightfoot takes the opposite name, observing that the rabbis were divided over whether Abraham was called a Hebrew from Heber or from having come over the river.

Two ask why the office was not created sooner. Barnes answers that it was better deferred until the need was manifest, since while the church was small the apostles could distribute its alms themselves; and he draws a rule from it, that the temporal affairs of a church should never be much entrusted to its clergy, who ought to be free of all suspicion in money. Calvin reaches the same place by the proverb that good laws take their beginning of evil manners. Had deacons been proposed before any necessity appeared, the people would not have been ready, the apostles would have seemed to avoid labour, and many would not have given so liberally into other men's hands; the faithful had first to be convinced by experience.

On the murmuring Henry is of two minds at once. It does the heart good to see the disciples multiplied, since the opposition that met the preaching contributed to its success, this infant church multiplying, like the infant Jewish church in Egypt, the more it was afflicted; yet it casts a damp that the multiplying itself became the occasion of discord, when hitherto they had all been with one accord. Wesley makes it the first breach, asks how short a time pure Christianity remained in the world, and sees in this partiality and murmuring the seeds of a general persecution, which he takes to be at once penal and medicinal. Robertson keeps to the word itself, onomatopoetic, the secret grumblings that buzz away until they are heard.

The apostles' answer draws admiration. Ellicott finds singular tact in it, since they neither resent the suspicion nor trouble to vindicate themselves, and thinks they may have remembered how Moses delegated part of his authority; the action of the multitude, he adds, agrees strikingly with the Greek sense of the word for assembly, in which every citizen has his share and his vote. Calvin sees patience in their not being more moved and prudence in their meeting the evil early, since a division that has gathered strength is a wound hard to cure; the meeting proves the church governed by order, the apostles holding chief authority yet imparting their counsels to the people. Barnes and Clarke agree that the words rendered not reason mean not pleasing, the sense required being not fit or proper.

The tables are disputed. Ellicott observes that the word served for the money-changers' tables and so suits relief given in coin or in kind; Robertson thinks it means rather the tables of the daily distribution of food, and judges that the office of deacon, as distinct from bishop or elder, probably grew out of this incident, though he reports Furneaux as certain that the seven are not the later deacons, without saying why. Wesley divides the work as the early church did, preaching the primary business of apostles and bishops, the care of the poor and the widows the secondary; when any of the seven afterwards preached, he holds, they did so on another commission. Gill counts the growth behind the trouble, from the hundred and twenty to three thousand, then five thousand, then multitudes of men and women.
3:
The word for looking out is read as an election, and most make a point of it. Gill notes that the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic all render it choose, and infers that deacons must belong to the church they serve and be chosen by the common suffrages of its people. Barnes draws the same conclusion and adds the motive: the right of selection rests with the church and not the ministry, and by leaving it there the apostles could never be charged with partiality or with embezzling what they administered themselves. Calvin puts it sharply, that it is tyrannous for one man to make ministers at his pleasure, and complains that the deacons of Rome are left no office but handling the paten and chalice.

Lightfoot dissents on who did the choosing. He derives the office from the synagogue, where three such officers had charge of the poor, and supposes the seven were chosen out of the hundred and twenty named earlier, and by them only rather than by the whole church. On the number he declines to be curious, though he recalls the seven good men of the city whom the rabbis often mention. Barnes and Clarke agree there is no mystery in it, Barnes calling it merely convenient and denying that any church is bound to the number now, Clarke guessing that each man took his day, so that the widows had a superintendent for every day of the week.

Ellicott alone looks outside Judaism for the number. It may come from the general reverence for seven, he allows, but equally from the Roman Hellenists, among whom a guild called the Seven Stewards arranged the banquets held in honour of the gods, something like the later love-feasts, and he thinks it a striking coincidence that these too were appointed to relieve the priests of a duty grown too heavy. On the qualifications he makes a theological point, that the apostles plainly did not confine the Spirit's working to prophecy and tongues, since wherever wisdom and charity are wanted there is need of a grace that lifts men above prejudice and passion.

Robertson and Clarke both stop at a variant in the last clause. The better reading is a future, we shall appoint, so the apostles' act follows the church's choice and is promised as a certainty, where the received text has a subjunctive that leaves it open. Robertson glosses the good report as a standing reputation held alongside the spiritual gifts. Clarke takes the wisdom required to be prudence and economy, since mere piety could not serve where so many had to be pleased; Wesley agrees that it is no light matter to dispense even the temporal goods of a church, and wishes ordinary ministers in every age had acted as much in concert with their people.

On the apostles' own portion the comment turns to the force of the verb. Clarke calls it emphatic, that they will steadfastly and invariably attend, and adds that even apostles could not live without prayer, having no independent graces: a minister who does not pray much studies in vain. Calvin hears in the word the sense of being fastened to a thing, and warns pastors not to think their duty done because they have spent some time each day in teaching; they join prayer to it, he says, not because they alone ought to pray but because they have peculiar cause. Barnes cannot decide whether public or private prayer is meant, though the link with preaching inclines him to the public; Ellicott takes it to cover the church's whole public worship as well as private intercession, and observes that these men are never called deacons in the New Testament but only the Seven. Wesley calls the pair of duties the proper business of a bishop, who speaks to God in prayer and to men as an ambassador for Christ.
5:
That all seven bear Greek names is noticed by all, but not read the same way. Robertson calls them undoubtedly Hellenists and finds consummate wisdom in it, since the murmuring came from that side and seven of their own were now set over their widows; the trouble, he adds, stayed settled. Wesley agrees, and thinks the proselyte was chosen because proselytes would the more readily apply to him. Ellicott calls the inference natural but not necessary, allows that the Hebrews may have voted generously to give the other party its own representatives, and suggests the order of names may be the order of election, Stephen heading the poll. Lightfoot dissents outright: he would call them Hebrews who understood Greek, that being why the care of the Hellenists fell to them, since it is hardly supposable that Stephen pleaded before the Sanhedrin in a tongue not his own.

Nicolas draws a second dispute. Calvin reports that the ancient writers affirm with great consent that this is the man of the Revelation, author of a filthy sect, and draws the moral that we must not be negligent in choosing ministers, since hypocrisy deceives even the vigilant. Barnes names the same Fathers but answers that the evidence is not clear. Clarke reports both sides, adding that Clement of Alexandria gives Nicolas a good character, and that he is the only proselyte listed, the rest being taken for native Jews. Lightfoot offers a way out, deriving the sect's name instead from a phrase meaning let us eat together.

Stephen is singled out before his story begins. Calvin will not let faith be separated from the Spirit, as though faith were not itself the Spirit's gift; by the Spirit, he says, Luke means Stephen's other graces, zeal, wisdom, uprightness and integrity of conscience, the rest being less commended as inferior to him. Leo, preaching on the martyrs, sets the matter under the love of God and neighbour, in which the martyrs stand nearest to the Lord in imitation as in likeness of suffering; and though no man's kindness can equal the love that redeemed us, they did great service in showing that death and the cross need not be terrible to any follower.

The laying on of hands is the first in the book, and they weigh what it does. Barnes says it conveyed no power but designated where the commission came from, so men chosen by the church still took their authority from the apostles. Calvin agrees that the rite has of itself no force, the effect depending on the Spirit alone, as should be thought of ceremonies generally, and that prayer was added lest the sign be vain. Ellicott is warmer, finding its symbolism in the concentration of prayer upon one man, and notes that it has kept its place beside Baptism and the Supper. Lightfoot notes what is missing on the other side: the rabbis made synagogue officers with a form of words and no imposition of hands.

The chapter turns on the growth that follows. Gill reads the episode as a stratagem of Satan that failed, issuing in better discipline and a wider spread of the gospel, and Wesley says simply that the hindrances were removed. Calvin distinguishes two ways the word grows, by new disciples and by the progress of those already taught, takes this of the first, and restrains the increase to Jerusalem, where alone there was yet a settled body. Robertson marks two imperfects keeping pace and a third for the priests obeying one after another, and notes that they were usually Sadducees, so it was a sad day for Annas and Caiaphas. Clarke calls their conversion one of the greatest miracles of grace, and draws from it that sinners are converted not by miracles but by the preaching of Christ crucified; Ellicott connects it with Stephen's new teaching, that the time for sacrifices had passed.
8:
A textual variant opens the paragraph. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all report that the better manuscripts read grace rather than faith, Clarke noting how many versions carry it and that some copies join both, Robertson preferring it and finding in the four words a picture of remarkable attractiveness. Gill keeps faith but records the same variant, and takes the power to mean at once the power to preach, to defend the gospel, to bear indignities and to work miracles. Calvin enters a caution against pressing the word full: we are not to imagine perfection of faith, since Scripture commonly calls those full of God's gifts who are abundantly endued with them.

Henry makes the fullness an argument. Those full of faith are full of power, because by faith the power of God is engaged for us, and Stephen's faith so filled him that it left no room for unbelief; he adds that Stephen had not thought the office of distributing charity beneath him, and being faithful in a little was entrusted with more. Chrysostom sees the promotion differently. Even among the seven one was pre-eminent and won the first prize, drawing greater grace upon himself though the ordination was common to them all; and he observes that Stephen worked no signs until he became publicly known, which shows that grace alone is not sufficient but that there must be ordination too, a further access of the Spirit beyond what came by baptism.

The synagogue of the Libertines sets the commentators counting. Ellicott reads the structure of the sentence as putting Libertines, Cyrenians and Alexandrians in one synagogue and the men of Cilicia and Asia in another; he takes the Libertini for emancipated Roman Jews, descendants of Pompey's captives settled across the Tiber, recalls that Tacitus has four thousand of that class banished to Sardinia, and thinks Stephen himself sprang from them. Wesley makes it a single synagogue serving all these nations, and guesses that Saul of Cilicia belonged to it and perhaps Gamaliel presided over it. Robertson allows either two groups or five, since the article is used twice, and says plainly that Luke's language is not clear. Clarke prefers Bishop Pearce's solution, that since the Cyrenians lived in Libya and the Alexandrians nearby, the Libertines should be looked for in the same part of the world rather than at Rome. Calvin supposes instead that Roman freedmen built the synagogue at their own charge for Jews arriving from the provinces.

The number of synagogues in the city is disputed in passing. Barnes repeats the common estimate of four hundred and eighty, on older authority; Robertson answers that Schuerer calls that figure a Talmudic myth, and that while there were many, no one knows how many.

What broke against Stephen is the last point. Calvin traces the shape of persecution, that the wicked first assault the gospel with the tongue, and only when disputing fails do they fly to slander and tumult and at last to violence; he had already called this a new combat, the church assaulted in the person of one man. Robertson keeps the imperfect, that they continued to have no strength to take a stand, and pictures Stephen knocking them down, Saul included, as fast as they got up. Ellicott finds it remarkable that Stephen is the first Christian teacher of whom wisdom is specially predicated, a word the Gospels reserve for our Lord. On the spirit they parted company. Barnes denies it means the Holy Spirit and makes it Stephen's own energy and ardour, since evident sincerity convinces the mass of men further than the ablest argument delivered coldly; Clarke holds it was the Holy Spirit and its power irresistible, so that they must either yield to its teaching or be confounded by its truth. Gill notes only that one ancient copy adds the words which was in him.
11:
The suborning is put in legal terms. Barnes defines it as procuring a man to swear falsely, and explains how it was managed: not by open falsehood but by perverting Stephen's doctrine and putting their own inferences forward as what he had maintained, which he calls the common way of opposing a doctrine one dislikes. Clarke says they made underhand work with profligates who for money would swear anything. Robertson notes what the charge reveals: Moses stands before God in it, practically on a par, and blasphemy was punished by stoning.

The appeal to the crowd is new. Robertson says they shook the people together like an earthquake, the first record of the masses turning hostile to the disciples; the elders and scribes are reached, but not the Sadducees. Gill explains why the people were so easily wrought on, nothing provoking them like a hint that the rites of Moses were slighted. Clarke is bitterest here: the elders and scribes made themselves one with the basest of the people and brought a good man, without form of justice, before a council ready for every evil work.

Calvin reads the turn to witnesses as a defeat confessed. Overcome by the power of the Spirit they give over disputing and fall back on slander, striving against their own conscience, since nothing is more unfitting than to rest a cause upon lies; even a guilty man, he adds, must not be borne down by false testimony, though hypocrites who shroud themselves in zeal give themselves leave. Barnes asks why the witnesses are called false if they only reported what Stephen said, and answers that even so they perverted his meaning, doubting he ever used those words. Clarke thinks they had likely heard something to that effect, true enough in the spirit from which it came, but gave it a false colouring; Wesley puts it shortest, that so they might have heard him, but the consequence they drew would not follow.

What Stephen actually taught is reconstructed from the charge. Ellicott holds the accusation false but its falsehood a distortion of truth, as with the charges against our Lord, each count resting on words really spoken; Stephen must have taught that the Temple's days were numbered and the Law was to give way to a higher revelation, and his accusers would think it natural that the man who foretold the fall should be its agent. He takes the customs for the whole system of the Law, its ritual, circumcision, the Sabbath and the clean and unclean. Robertson calls the quoted saying the only direct testimony and evidently wrong, but grants that Stephen had caught the spirit of what Jesus said at the well, that God is spirit and may be worshipped anywhere: inflammable material, easily misrepresented. Calvin grants the charge was not laid for nothing, since Stephen had taught the abrogating of the law, and notes that Christ too had to clear himself of the same wresting.

The face at the end is read as a verdict. Lightfoot says God bore witness by a miracle to this holy man's innocence, showing he had done Moses no wrong by making his face shine as Moses's own had. Clarke fills in the background from the rabbis, who often have God distinguish eminent men by a glory in the face, one describing Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh with faces like the sun and words like thunder. Calvin keeps it sober: this is said not of his natural face but of his bearing at that moment, for where the arraigned are commonly pale and stammering, in Stephen there appeared a certain majesty. Ellicott traces the description to the impression made on Paul and passed to Luke. Robertson observes that even his enemies saw it, and asks where Peter and John were, since Stephen stands before the council alone as Jesus had, with no Gamaliel to interpose.
